source.citation: Glasgow PD, Ferris R, Bleakley CM. Cold Water Immersion in the Management of Delayed-Onset Muscle Soreness: Is Dose Important? A Randomised Controlled Trial. Phys Ther Sport. 2014;15(4):228-233. doi:10.1016/j.ptsp.2014.01.002.

researchEvidence.populationLabel: Healthy adults after eccentric exercise intended to provoke delayed-onset muscle soreness
researchEvidence.durationLabel: Single recovery session with outcomes followed for 96 hours

protocolEvidence.headline: Different post-exercise cold-water doses were compared, but no protocol clearly outperformed the others on DOMS outcomes.
protocolEvidence.implication: Supports conservative dose language for recovery-focused use and cautions against claiming a clearly optimal plunge recipe from this trial alone.
protocolEvidence.caveat: Exercise-induced DOMS model in healthy participants; not a general cold-plunge use case.

whyItMatters: Useful for implementation guardrails because it directly compares several cold-water dosing options after exercise, but it remains a sports-recovery DOMS study rather than a general cold-plunge wellbeing trial.
protocolTakeaway: Use only as adjacent dose context for post-exercise recovery discussions. Do not treat it as direct evidence that an ordinary cold plunge improves soreness or recovery in non-exercise users.
murphTakeaway: Use only as adjacent dose context for post-exercise recovery discussions. The trial mostly showed no statistically significant between-group advantage, so it should narrow overconfident temperature-or-duration claims rather than support them.
body:
This source is included for **Recovery dose trial**.



## Findings

Fifty healthy participants were randomized to seated rest or one of four cold/contrast recovery protocols after eccentric exercise: short contrast immersion, short intermittent cold-water immersion at 10°C, 10 minutes at 10°C, or 10 minutes at 6°C.

Outcomes included muscle soreness, pain on stretch, active range of movement, muscle strength, and serum creatine kinase through 96 hours. The 10-minute 6°C condition showed the lowest soreness and pain-on-stretch values, but differences were not statistically significant, and there were no significant between-group differences for the other outcomes.

No dropouts or adverse effects were reported in the abstracted record. The main limitation is that the trial addresses exercise-induced muscle damage management, not a general-purpose cold plunge protocol.



## Why it matters

Useful for implementation guardrails because it directly compares several cold-water dosing options after exercise, but it remains a sports-recovery DOMS study rather than a general cold-plunge wellbeing trial.



## Potential experiment signals

- muscle soreness

- pain on stretch

- range of motion

- muscle strength

- creatine kinase



## Protocol takeaway

Use only as adjacent dose context for post-exercise recovery discussions. Do not treat it as direct evidence that an ordinary cold plunge improves soreness or recovery in non-exercise users.



## Claim use

Context only. This trial can inform adjacent recovery dose wording and endpoint choice, but it should not be used as direct support for general cold-plunge efficacy claims.

body:
This source is included for **Open-water failure modes and deaths**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Narrative review (2014).
- **People studied or addressed:** Open-water swimming participants and event-safety context.
- **Role in Murph:** adjacent fatality/safety context.
- **Directness to Cold Plunge:** adjacent variant safety context rather than direct plunge evidence.
- **Population mismatch:** High: the review centers on open-water swimming, event organization, and exertional water movement rather than stationary plunges.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** swimming or treading-water demands, panic, loss of coordination, cardiac symptoms, environmental supervision.

## Findings

- The review summarizes hazards of open-water swimming and presents event-organization guidance intended to reduce risk.
- It notes that better understanding of immersion responses and precursors to cardiac events may reduce deaths, because cardiac events appear to be a major cause of death in open-water swimming.
- That makes the source useful for safety boundaries, but it should remain clearly separate from the stationary cold-plunge protocol.

## Limitations

- Adjacent open-water endurance/swimming context, not static plunges.
- Narrative review rather than direct plunge trial.

## Why it matters

It helps keep the page from confusing open-water swimming fatalities and endurance problems with a controlled stationary plunge, while still preserving real fatality context.

## Potential experiment signals

- swimming or treading-water demands
- panic
- loss of coordination
- cardiac symptoms
- environmental supervision

## Protocol takeaway

Keep open-water swimming and static cold plunges separate. Use this source to support no-swim/no-solo warnings, not to make direct claims about brief home plunges.

## Claim use

`safety-only`. Keep this source on the safety/context boundary rather than using it as direct efficacy support for the protocol.

body:
This source is included for **Resistance-exercise recovery trial**.



## Findings

In a randomized crossover design, 10 physically active men completed high-intensity resistance exercise followed by either 10 minutes of 10°C cold-water immersion or 10 minutes of low-intensity cycling recovery.

Cold-water immersion did not improve maximal muscle function at 2 or 4 hours, but during a 6-hour submaximal squat test participants completed greater total load in the final three sets after cold-water immersion than after active recovery. The study also reported lower plasma myoglobin, higher IL-6, and sustained reductions in intramuscular temperature after immersion.

These mixed findings matter for protocol boundaries: the study supports some task-specific recovery effects, but it does not support a broad claim that cold plunges universally restore strength or performance.



## Why it matters

Useful for preserving mixed recovery findings. It shows why some cold-water immersion benefits appear task-specific and do not automatically extend to all performance or recovery outcomes.



## Potential experiment signals

- submaximal muscle function

- jump height

- isometric squat strength

- muscle soreness

- myoglobin

- IL-6



## Protocol takeaway

Use only as adjacent resistance-exercise recovery context. It should not be generalized into a claim that a cold plunge broadly improves all post-exercise recovery metrics.



## Claim use

Context only. Appropriate as mixed adjacent resistance-exercise evidence, not as direct support for a general cold-plunge protocol.

body:
This source is included for **population_boundary_adjacent_claims**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** 12-month randomized placebo-controlled trial during resistance training (2015).
- **People studied or addressed:** Postmenopausal women participating in supervised resistance training.
- **Intervention/exposure:** Creatine approximately 0.1 g/kg/day during resistance training.
- **Comparator/control:** Placebo during resistance training.
- **Duration/follow-up:** 12 months.
- **Role in Murph:** context-only / adjacent_variant.

## Findings

**Findings:** In postmenopausal women randomized to creatine or placebo during resistance training, the creatine group was reported to attenuate femoral-neck BMD loss and increase femoral-shaft subperiosteal width; 47 women were randomized and 33 were analyzed at 12 months [source_artifact:pmid-25386713].

## Why it matters

Bone claims are tempting in older-women copy, so this source needs to remain in a bone-specific adjacent bucket. [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]

## Potential experiment signals

DXA and bone-geometry outcomes belong in a separate bone-health protocol, not in default Murph tracking [source_artifact:pmid-25386713].

## Protocol takeaway

Use only for bone-specific variant synthesis; do not cite for default protocol outcomes. [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]

## Key limitations and population mismatch

- Postmenopausal women only [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]
- Small analyzed sample after attrition [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]
- Bone-health endpoints are not default gym protocol endpoints [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]
- Concurrent resistance training complicates attribution [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]
- Population mismatch: Postmenopausal bone-health trial is adjacent to, not direct evidence for, the default healthy-adult gym protocol. [source_artifact:pmid-25386713]

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Mixed and null clinical evidence**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Multicenter randomized cardiac-rehabilitation trial (2015).
- **People studied or addressed:** Stable coronary artery disease patients (200 participants).
- **Role in Murph:** clinical context and overclaim control; does not confirm evidence; screened or supervised clinical exercise, not unsupervised home training.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy, session heart-rate fidelity, heart-rate recovery, symptoms and adherence.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

Larger CAD trial that prevents overclaiming HIIT superiority over moderate continuous training.

## What it found

**Findings:** The SAINTEX-CAD trial found that aerobic interval training and continuous training both improved exercise capacity in stable coronary artery disease patients. It did not show a clear superiority of interval training over continuous training. The finding is an overclaim guardrail for disease-treatment or superiority claims.

## How Murph should use it

This prevents claiming 4x4 is always better than moderate cardio.

Use to calibrate clinical context and avoid overclaiming superiority; do not treat supervised disease-population results as direct home-protocol proof.

## Important limits

The setting was supervised clinical rehabilitation, not a general wellness experiment.

The safe interpretation is narrower than “4x4 is always better.” Keep the population, supervision level, comparator, and exact interval dose visible before applying this source to a home wearable experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This helps explain where the 4x4 idea came from in supervised clinical exercise, but stable coronary artery disease patients are not the same as unscreened wellness users.

**Comparator or control:** Different morning bright-light duration within a multi-component protocol

**Endpoints:** Circadian phase advance

**Effect estimates or direction:** Direction: phase advance targeted with combined intervention; light-only effect not isolated in extracted materials.

**Safety/adverse events:** No adverse events extracted from this batch; melatonin co-intervention means safety boundaries may differ from light-only protocols.

**Limitations:**
- Multi-component intervention.
- Not outdoor daylight.
- Participant count/effect estimates not extracted.

**Potential experiment signals:** morning bright light duration, melatonin timing, shifted sleep, phase advance.

body:
This source is included for **clinical_light_therapy_device_boundaries**.

**Findings:** Population: Depressive inpatients treated in two hospital environments with different daylight availability. Intervention/exposure: Higher daylight-availability hospital environment with approximately three-fold greater accumulated light availability. Comparator/control: Lower daylight-availability hospital environment. Duration/follow-up: Index hospitalization Endpoints: length of hospitalization. Effect/direction: Median hospitalization fell from 14 days (IQR 8-19; n=101) in the lower-daylight hospital to 11 days (IQR 6-15; n=106) in the higher-daylight hospital; significance was reported for the whole group, while subgroup analyses were not significant. Safety/adverse events: No adverse events were extracted.

**Why it matters:** Clinical daylight-availability context supports separating architectural/daylight evidence from outdoor-habit evidence.

**Potential experiment signals:** hospital length of stay, facility daylight availability

**Protocol takeaway:** Hospital-level observational exposure cannot support causal outdoor morning-light claims.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: Clinical inpatient depression rather than healthy users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** Retrospective hospital-level comparison; no individual light-dose measurement; subgroups not statistically significant; not outdoor exposure.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **body_weight_water_gi**.

**Findings:**
- Forty rheumatoid arthritis patients were randomized to creatine or placebo.
- Creatine increased appendicular lean mass by 0.52 ± 0.13 kg versus placebo (p=0.004) and the lean-mass change concurred with intracellular water gain of 0.64 ± 0.22 L (p=0.035).
- Creatine did not improve isometric knee extensor strength, handgrip strength, or objectively assessed physical function versus placebo; no treatment-related adverse effects were reported in available summaries.

**Why it matters:**
Shows lean-mass/water signal in a clinical population while preserving null function outcomes.

**Potential experiment signals:**
- population / rheumatoid arthritis
- biomarker / appendicular lean mass
- biomarker / intracellular water
- outcome / knee extensor strength
- outcome / handgrip strength
- outcome / objective physical function

**Protocol takeaway:**
Clinical body-composition context; do not generalize to default healthy-adult outcomes.

**Population mismatch / boundary:**
Rheumatoid arthritis patients; clinical supervised context.

**Limitations:**
- Clinical RA population; disease and cachexia mechanisms differ from healthy users.
- Function outcomes were null despite lean-mass change.
- Not a default protocol RCT.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Exact or close 4x4 trials**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Three-arm 4x4 versus 1x4 versus moderate-continuous trial (2016).
- **People studied or addressed:** Overweight and obese adults (30 participants).
- **Role in Murph:** direct fit for the exact 4x4 claim and the clearest direct variant-separation paper.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy, session heart-rate fidelity, variant separation.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

This is the direct paper that most clearly says classic 4x4 and low-volume 1x4 are not the same thing.

## What it found

**Findings:** Thirty overweight and obese adults were randomized to 6 weeks of 4x4, 1x4, or 45-minute moderate continuous training. Only the 4x4 group improved VO2max clearly more than the other two groups—about a 10% gain versus about 3% in the 1x4 and moderate groups—and estimated stroke volume improved only after 4x4. That makes this one of the strongest direct reasons to keep the standard four-interval dose separate from low-volume HIIT.

## How Murph should use it

Use it to support both the main fitness claim and the rule that 4x4 and 1x4 should not be merged into one bucket.

## Important limits

The comparison was still a small structured training study in a specific population, not a free-living wearable experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This is the paper that most directly says “4x4 is not the same as 1x4.”

Youth male athletes; direct water effect but not full default adult population.

**Limitations:**
- Very small sample.
- Under-20 male soccer players may not generalize to adults, women, or sedentary users.
- Short loading protocol only.

body:
This source is included for **clinical_light_therapy_device_boundaries**.

**Findings:** Population: Adults aged 19-60 years with nonseasonal major depressive disorder of at least moderate severity. Intervention/exposure: Bright light treatment alone or combined with fluoxetine. Comparator/control: Fluoxetine alone and placebo/sham-placebo condition. Duration/follow-up: 8 weeks Endpoints: MADRS response, remission, treatment-emergent adverse events. Effect/direction: At endpoint, response/remission were 33.3%/30.0% for placebo, 29.0%/19.4% for fluoxetine, 50.0%/43.8% for light, and 75.9%/58.6% for combination. Combination therapy was superior to placebo for MADRS response (p=.005; NNT 2.4) and remission (p=.02; NNT 3.5). Safety/adverse events: All treatments were generally well tolerated with few significant differences in treatment-emergent adverse events in accessible extraction.

**Why it matters:** Landmark clinical-device evidence outside SAD boundaries.

**Potential experiment signals:** MADRS response, remission, NNT, treatment-emergent adverse events

**Protocol takeaway:** Clinical bright-light treatment and combination pharmacotherapy are not equivalent to an outdoor morning-light habit.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: Moderate/severe nonseasonal MDD under trial treatment, not general outdoor-light users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** Nonseasonal MDD clinical sample; device-based bright light; single SSRI comparator; trial duration relatively short; not outdoor daylight.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

One hundred participants completed a jump-plus-Wingate exercise protocol and were then assigned to control recovery, 5 minutes at 9°C, 5 minutes at 14°C, 15 minutes at 9°C, or 15 minutes at 14°C.

This source is included for **Emergency and thermoregulation boundary**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Clinical review (2016).
- **People studied or addressed:** Clinical heat- and cold-stress illness context.
- **Role in Murph:** clinical emergency boundary.
- **Directness to Cold Plunge:** clinical emergency-boundary context rather than direct protocol evidence.
- **Population mismatch:** High for ordinary cold-plunge dosing; this source addresses clinical illness recognition and management rather than healthy-user protocol optimization.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** shivering severity, confusion or mental-status change, respiratory depression, cardiac rhythm symptoms, hypotension/collapse.

## Findings

- The review states that hypothermia below 35°C is a medical emergency.
- It describes severe hypothermia as potentially involving shivering, respiratory depression, cardiac dysrhythmias, impaired mental function, hypotension, and progression to cardiac arrest or coma.
- Management is framed in clinical terms—warming, hydration, and cardiovascular support—so the source belongs in emergency-stop boundaries, not in protocol dosing.

## Limitations

- Clinical review rather than direct plunge study.
- High mismatch with healthy-user dose setting.

## Why it matters

This is the best batch source for drawing the line between normal discomfort and a genuine cold emergency that needs prompt escalation.

- shivering severity
- confusion or mental-status change
- respiratory depression
- cardiac rhythm symptoms
- hypotension/collapse

## Protocol takeaway

Use this source for emergency-stop language, not for dosing. Confusion, collapse, respiratory depression, or significant cardiac symptoms are escalation signs, not adaptation signs.

This source is included for **Cold-shock physiology**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Editorial review (1989).

- **Role in Murph:** direct safety context.
- **Directness to Cold Plunge:** direct safety-boundary context for plunge entry.

## Findings

- The review’s central claim is that cold-shock responses can cause serious incapacitation or death well before a person becomes hypothermic.
- It therefore shifts attention from late core-cooling narratives to the first-minute respiratory and cardiovascular hazard window.
- This is useful for safety framing, but it is not a dosing or benefit source.

## Limitations

- Review article rather than a pooled quantitative experiment.
- Predates much of the later habituation and winter-swimming literature.
- Does not by itself specify a beginner dose or home-use protocol.

## Why it matters

- palpitations or dizziness on entry

## Protocol takeaway

body:
This source is included for **Temperature comparison recovery trial**.



## Findings

Sixty healthy male participants were randomized to passive recovery, 15 minutes of cold-water immersion at 9°C, or 15 minutes at 14°C after an eccentric exercise protocol.

Markers included creatine kinase, muscle soreness, pain threshold, perceived recovery, and maximal voluntary isometric contraction up to 96 hours. The abstract reports large time effects for all outcomes, earlier immediate soreness recovery in the cold-water groups, and earlier maximal-force recovery in the 14°C group compared with 9°C and control, but no significant overall group or group-by-time effects.

The authors reported no evidence of a clear dose-response relationship and no deleterious effects on performance. That makes this a useful adjacent implementation source, but not strong support for a single best cold-plunge temperature.



## Why it matters

Directly compares two cold-water temperatures after exercise, which is useful for adjacent implementation nuance, but the population and outcome set are specific to sports recovery.



## Potential experiment signals

- muscle soreness

- pain threshold

- perceived recovery

- maximal isometric strength

- creatine kinase



## Protocol takeaway

Use as adjacent recovery-temperature context only. It does not show a robust dose-response relationship that should be converted into a general cold-plunge prescription.



## Claim use

Context only. This trial can calibrate adjacent recovery-temperature claims, but it should not be promoted as direct support for general cold-plunge efficacy or a universally optimal water temperature.

body:
This source is included for **Cold-shower adjacent variant**.

## Findings
- **Source kind / design:** Randomized controlled trial (journal_article).
- **Population:** Adults aged 18-65 without severe comorbidity and not routinely taking cold showers.
- **Participant count:** 3018 (reported).
- **Intervention or exposure:** Usual hot shower followed by 30, 60, or 90 seconds of cold water daily for 30 days, then optional continuation for 60 days.
- **Comparator or control:** No cold-shower control group.
- **Duration or follow-up:** 30 consecutive intervention days plus 60 optional follow-on days
- **Endpoints:** Illness days and sickness absence from work.
- **Effect estimate or direction:** Routine cold showering reduced self-reported sickness absence but not illness days; the reported incidence-rate ratio for sickness absence was about 0.71, and the different cold-duration arms did not clearly separate.
- **Adverse events or safety notes:** No related serious adverse events were reported in retrieved summaries.
- **Limitations:** Cold showering is a materially different modality from deliberate cold plunge in water depth, body surface area exposed, and likely thermal load.
- **Population mismatch:** This source does not cleanly match a default self-directed deliberate cold-plunge protocol.

A large RCT gives more behavioral signal than most adjacent-variant studies, while still requiring strict modality separation.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

Larger HFrEF trial that did not confirm clear HIIT superiority and highlighted intensity-fidelity issues.

## What it found

**Findings:** This heart-failure trial did not confirm a clear durable superiority of HIIT over moderate training or recommended regular exercise. It also highlighted that participants often missed the prescribed high-intensity target. The finding warns that clinical 4x4-style protocols need supervision and intensity checks.

## How Murph should use it

Use it as a guardrail: the intended dose matters, and clinical outcomes do not automatically transfer to home 4x4.

Use to calibrate clinical context and avoid overclaiming superiority; do not treat supervised disease-population results as direct home-protocol proof.

## Important limits

Heart-failure participants need clinician-directed exercise decisions.

The safe interpretation is narrower than “4x4 is always better.” Keep the population, supervision level, comparator, and exact interval dose visible before applying this source to a home wearable experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This helps explain where the 4x4 idea came from in supervised clinical exercise, but heart-failure patients with reduced ejection fraction are not the same as unscreened wellness users.

Low-volume 1x4 HIIT evidence that should not be treated as the same as standard 4x4.

## What it found

**Findings:** The trial found that low-volume HIIT could improve metabolic-syndrome severity. Its protocol was a lower-volume variant rather than classic four-by-four-minute intervals. The finding is useful cardiometabolic context but should stay separate from Norwegian 4x4 dosing.

Useful for variant separation; do not merge it into the standard four-interval protocol.

Low-volume protocols have different burden, dose, and interpretation.

This is useful nearby evidence, but it should not be mixed into the direct claim that the standard four-interval recipe will improve a user's wearable fitness score.

This source is included for **Safety, contraindication, and population-boundary evidence**.

**Findings:** The review screened a large light-therapy literature and included 43 articles. This source is included for **clinical_light_therapy_device_boundaries**.

**Findings:** Population: Adults with acute bipolar depression. Intervention/exposure: Bright light therapy as adjunctive treatment, one hour every morning for two weeks. Comparator/control: Dim red light therapy control. Duration/follow-up: 2 weeks Endpoints: HAMD-17 reduction response, QIDS-SR16 onset day, switch into hypomania/mania, adverse events. Effect/direction: Seventy-four participants were randomized and 63 completed. Response rates were 78.19% for BLT versus 43.33% for control (p<0.01), and median onset day in the BLT group was 4.33 days. Safety/adverse events: No participants experienced BLT-emergent hypomania; no serious adverse events were reported in the accessible extract.

**Why it matters:** Core bipolar safety and clinical boundary source.

**Potential experiment signals:** HAMD-17 response, QIDS onset, hypomania/mania switch, adverse events

**Protocol takeaway:** Short-term supervised bipolar treatment results should not be generalized to self-directed morning light in bipolar-spectrum users.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: Acute bipolar depression, not general outdoor protocol users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** Short duration; single-blind design; acute bipolar depression population; device-based adjunctive clinical treatment.

- lean tissue mass

**Limitations:**
- Older-adult RT synthesis; do not generalize effect size to all adults.

body:
This clinical review is the main general reference for how pulse oximetry works and why it can be wrong.

For Murph, the most important takeaway is that SpO₂ should be interpreted as an estimate and as a trend signal. This source is included for **safety_boundaries**.

**Source key:** `source_artifact:pmid-29348073`.

**Findings:** Across 41 studies describing 799 bipolar-disorder patients treated with light therapy, 7 (0.9%) switched into mania and 11 (1.4%) switched into hypomania; switch detection varied by assessment method, and the rapid-cycling subgroup had a higher reported switch rate.

**Potential experiment signals:** switch into mania, switch into hypomania, rapid-cycling subgroup, assessment-method sensitivity.

**Protocol takeaway:** Morning outdoor-light guidance should include a bipolar/mania screening boundary and monitoring for elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, agitation, or mixed symptoms.

- **Participant count:** 799 (patients_in_reviewed_studies).
- **Population:** People with bipolar disorder treated with antidepressant light therapy across 41 studies.
- **Intervention or exposure:** Light therapy for bipolar depression, including morning light therapy.
- **Comparator or control:** Historical rates and study-level synthesis; not a single controlled comparator.
- **Duration or follow-up:** Historical literature review; treatment durations varied.
- **Endpoints:** switch into mania; switch into hypomania; rapid-cycling subgroup; assessment-method sensitivity
- **Effect estimates or direction:** Across 41 studies describing 799 bipolar-disorder patients treated with light therapy, 7 (0.9%) switched into mania and 11 (1.4%) switched into hypomania; switch detection varied by assessment method, and the rapid-cycling subgroup had a higher reported switch rate.
- **Adverse events or safety notes:** Manic or hypomanic switch is a key safety boundary even if aggregate rates were low; rapid-cycling bipolar disorder is a particular caution signal.
- **Population mismatch:** Bipolar-depression treatment population; cannot be generalized to all users, but it is directly relevant to bipolar safety screening.
- **Directness to Morning Outdoor Light Exposure:** Safety boundary. This source does not establish direct efficacy for the protocol variant.

**Directness and boundaries:** The review addresses clinical light therapy for bipolar depression, not outdoor-morning-light wellness use.

- Historical review of heterogeneous studies.

body:
This source is included for **Skin/cosmetic large-area or full-body PBM sibling variant**.

**Findings:** This systematic review searched the literature on September 13, 2017 and included 31 original randomized controlled trials of LED treatments for skin conditions. Acne vulgaris, herpes simplex and zoster, and acute wound healing received grade B recommendations, while other skin conditions received only grade C or D recommendations. The review emphasized frequent design limitations, including small sample sizes often below 20 participants, absent blinding, no sham placebo, and widely varied treatment parameters. The authors also noted few incidences of adverse events across the included dermatology LED trials, but the review was not specific to whole-body red/NIR exposure.

**Why it matters:** It is useful for documenting the boundary between a generally reassuring dermatology safety profile and a weakly standardized efficacy literature.

**Potential experiment signals:** adverse events, sham control use, population fit, skin outcomes.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as safety-context and methodology-context only; do not turn this heterogeneous dermatology review into a direct whole-body PBM claim.

**Claim use:** `safety-only`.

This source is included for **Safety and contraindications**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Cardiac-rehabilitation systematic review and meta-analysis (2018).
- **People studied or addressed:** Cardiac-rehabilitation participants (about 953 pooled participants / 17 included studies).
- **Role in Murph:** supervised-setting context and safety boundary.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** screening context, symptoms, and stop-condition language.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

It helps explain why rehab evidence should make the safety language more careful, not more casual.

## What it found

**Findings:** This cardiac-rehabilitation synthesis found that HIIT and moderate continuous training both improved fitness inside supervised rehabilitation programs. That is useful when writing safety language, but the whole point is that screening, monitoring, and clinical escalation were built into the setting.

## How Murph should use it

Use it to reinforce that "worked in rehab" and "appropriate for an unscreened home user" are two different claims.

## Important limits

Cardiac rehab is a clinical care environment. That changes both the risk calculation and the meaning of a successful session.

## Plain-language takeaway

This is more about the boundary around safe supervision than about telling a healthy home user what result to expect.

body:
This source is included for **Clinical synthesis and overclaim guardrails**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Updated CAD and heart-failure aerobic-interval meta-analysis (2018).
- **People studied or addressed:** Patients with coronary artery disease or heart failure (about 1,080 pooled participants / 24 included studies).
- **Role in Murph:** clinical lineage and overclaim control; important context, but not direct home-protocol proof.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy, clinical secondary outcomes, safety and supervision context.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

It helps explain why 4x4 shows up so often in cardiac-rehab discussions without letting rehab evidence turn into general self-treatment advice.

## What it found

**Findings:** Across 24 studies and about 1,080 pooled clinical participants with coronary artery disease or heart failure, aerobic interval training often improved peak VO2 more than continuous training, especially in some CAD and HFrEF subgroup analyses, but many secondary outcomes were similar and the authors called for more evidence on safety and longer-term sustainability. That makes this useful lineage context, not proof that home 4x4 treats cardiovascular disease.

## How Murph should use it

Use it to calibrate the strength of the claim: interesting and sometimes favorable in supervised clinical care, but not clean permission to oversell home 4x4.

## Important limits

Clinical synthesis is valuable context, but the participants, medications, supervision, and escalation paths are not the same as those in an unscreened home experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This helps explain where 4x4 came from in cardiac rehab, but rehab patients are not the same as unscreened wellness users.

body:
This source is included for **clinical_light_therapy_device_boundaries**.

**Findings:** Population: Adolescents and young adults aged 13-24 years with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder. Intervention/exposure: Three weeks of post-awakening green bright light with sedentary activity or with scheduled morning activity. Comparator/control: Red light with sedentary activity or red light with morning activity. Duration/follow-up: 3-week intervention with 1- and 3-month follow-up Endpoints: sleep onset, wake time, sleep onset latency, total sleep time, daytime functioning. Effect/direction: No significant differences were found between treatment groups; interaction effects were non-significant. Sleep timing, sleep onset latency, and daytime function improved over time, but long-term relapse was common. Safety/adverse events: No adverse events were extracted from accessible abstract-level text.

**Why it matters:** Important null/mixed adjacent evidence for light-plus-activity protocols.

**Potential experiment signals:** sleep onset, wake time, sleep onset latency, daytime function, relapse

**Protocol takeaway:** Within-group improvement should not be interpreted as causal light efficacy.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: DSWPD clinical population, not general morning outdoor-light users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** No clear between-group advantage; active-light and activity conditions confounded; adolescent/young adult DSWPD population; device-based light rather than outdoor light.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Athlete sleep and recovery study**.



## Findings

Thirty recreationally trained men completed five days of heat training and were randomized to 90 minutes of cycling with passive recovery, the same training plus 15 minutes of cold-water immersion, or a shorter/higher-intensity heat-training condition with passive recovery.

Compared with baseline, heat training reduced total time asleep and perceived sleep quality and increased awake duration and wake after sleep onset. The abstract reports shorter sleep latency in the shorter-training arm versus the longer passive-recovery arm, but no differences between interventions for the other sleep variables.

The authors specifically note that adding cold-water immersion had minimal effect on sleep quantity or quality. That makes this a useful boundary source against overextending athlete-recovery sleep claims.



## Why it matters

Important for guarding sleep claims. This is a primary cold-water recovery sleep study, but the context is consecutive-day heat training in recreationally trained men, not ordinary cold-plunge use.



## Potential experiment signals

- total sleep time

- subjective sleep quality

- wake after sleep onset

- sleep latency



## Protocol takeaway

Use as athlete-only sleep context. It does not support a general claim that adding cold-water immersion improves sleep quantity or quality.



## Claim use

Context only. Appropriate for athlete heat-training sleep context, not for direct protocol claims that a cold plunge improves sleep.

body:
This source is included for **Dose, device, and implementation reporting**.

**Findings:** This perspective review explains that PBM began in laser-based research but now commonly uses non-coherent sources such as LEDs and broad-band lamps. It highlights practical LED advantages for whole-body and home-adjacent use, including fewer laser-specific safety considerations, easier home use, the ability to irradiate large tissue areas at once, wearable-device potential, and lower cost per mW. It also treats coherence and beam characteristics as meaningful device-class differences, so nominal wavelength matches alone should not be assumed to deliver equivalent exposure.

**Why it matters:** Whole-body PBM systems are usually LED-dominant. This source is therefore more useful for device translation and implementation boundaries than for efficacy claims.

**Potential experiment signals:** device class, beam spread, large-area coverage, home-usability constraints.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as background for LED-versus-laser interpretation and large-area treatment logic; do not promote it into a direct outcome claim.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Wearable or testable signals**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Systematic review of cardiac autonomic-control outcomes (2019).
- **People studied or addressed:** Healthy adults and cardiometabolic-risk participants (6 included studies).
- **Role in Murph:** recovery-context evidence, not a primary outcome source.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** HRV RMSSD, resting heart rate, and recovery interpretation.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

It helps stop people from turning HRV into the headline outcome when the literature is much messier than that.

## What it found

**Findings:** The autonomic-control review found HIIT-related changes in HRV and related markers were small, inconsistent, and hard to interpret across a small, heterogeneous literature. That is exactly why HRV should stay a recovery-context metric rather than the main verdict on whether 4x4 “worked.”

## How Murph should use it

Use it to keep recovery metrics in the right role: helpful context, not the main promise.

## Important limits

Autonomic measures are highly sensitive to sleep, illness, alcohol, stress, and overall training load, so a flat or worse HRV signal is not automatically proof that the protocol failed.

## Plain-language takeaway

HRV can help you notice under-recovery, but it is too noisy to be the headline outcome.

body:
This source is included for **free_living_observational_measurement**.

**Findings:** Among 133 healthy adults monitored for 7 days, all zeitgebers except evening physical activity correlated with at least five of ten sleep/rest-activity outcomes. Adjusted analyses linked later first and last indoor light and eating with later bedtimes and L5/M10 timing. Later first outdoor light was associated with longer sleep duration and lower MESOR, while higher morning physical activity predicted earlier in-bed/out-of-bed times, acrophase, and L5/M10 timing.

**Why it matters:** The paper anchors a practical measurement point: light is one of several daily zeitgebers, and timing may be as important as amount.

**Potential experiment signals:** first outdoor light time, last indoor light time, bedtime, sleep duration, inter-daily stability, L5/M10 timing.

**Population mismatch / directness:** Healthy adults are relevant, but the exposure was self-reported zeitgeber timing rather than prescribed outdoor morning light. Directness: `same_mechanism`.

**Limitations:** observational; self-reported light timing; multiple zeitgebers bundled; no randomized light assignment.

**Protocol takeaway:** Track first outdoor-light timing and other zeitgebers as context variables, but avoid claiming protocol efficacy from these associations.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Safety and contraindications**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Cardiovascular-disease HIIT safety systematic review (2018).
- **People studied or addressed:** Cardiovascular-disease rehabilitation patients (about 1,117 pooled participants / 23 included studies).
- **Role in Murph:** safety boundary; helps explain who should not treat vigorous intervals casually.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** symptoms and adherence, clinician-guidance boundaries, and stop-condition language.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

Low risk in cardiac rehab is not the same thing as no risk at home.

## What it found

**Findings:** Across 23 studies and more than 17,000 HIIT sessions in screened cardiovascular-disease populations, major adverse events were rare in supervised settings. That is reassuring as rehabilitation-context evidence, but it does not erase risk once screening, monitoring, medication review, and escalation plans disappear.

## How Murph should use it

Use it to justify strict screening questions and clinician-guidance boundaries for higher-risk users.

## Important limits

The participants were screened, supervised, and medically managed. That is exactly why this review is a boundary-setting source rather than a home-clearance source.

## Plain-language takeaway

Low risk in cardiac rehab is encouraging, but it is not permission to ignore symptoms or skip medical guidance when vigorous exercise may be risky.

**Findings:** In 12 DSWPD cases and 12 controls, DSWPD participants had later clock-time light patterns but, when aligned to DLMO, their light pattern was earlier. They had less daily phase-advancing light exposure, particularly in the late advancing window. Extracted group data showed worse PSQI and BDI, later sleep start/end/midpoint and later DLMO, while sleep duration was not different.

**Why it matters:** It is one of the more mechanistically aligned observational studies because it maps habitual light to DLMO and phase-advancing windows.

**Potential experiment signals:** DLMO, phase-advancing light exposure, PSQI, BDI, sleep midpoint.

**Population mismatch / directness:** Circadian-disorder population and small case-control sample; not a general adult protocol test. Directness: `adjacent_variant`.

**Limitations:** small sample; clinical population; observational; complex circadian alignment; not outdoor-specific.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as adjacent mechanistic timing context; do not promote it into direct protocol efficacy evidence.

body:
This source is included for **Dose, device, and implementation reporting**.

**Findings:** This review states that PBM still lacks agreement on clinical parameters and protocols, and it organizes the literature around wavelength, energy or fluence, power or irradiance, pulse mode, treatment duration, and repetition. It also distinguishes tissues with higher versus lower mitochondrial density, reinforcing that parameter-response relationships may not translate cleanly across targets. In practice, it is useful for whole-body PBM because it treats contradictory results as a parameter-reporting and dose-translation problem rather than as proof of a single uniform modality effect.

**Why it matters:** Whole-body light beds combine wavelength, irradiance, exposure time, geometry, and repetition into one delivered dose, so a source that explicitly warns about parameter sensitivity is more useful than generic PBM enthusiasm.

**Potential experiment signals:** wavelength, irradiance, fluence, session length, repeat-cadence tolerance.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as background for dose reporting, biphasic-dose caution, and tissue-context interpretation; do not promote it into a direct efficacy claim.

source.citation: Obayashi K, Yamagami Y, Kurumatani N, Saeki K. Pre-awake light exposure and sleep disturbances: findings from the HEIJO-KYO cohort. Sleep Med. 2019;54:121-125. doi:10.1016/j.sleep.2018.10.027. PMID:30554055.

whyItMatters: It is timing-specific and unusually close to the morning window, but the exposure occurred before waking and was associated with worse rather than better sleep outcomes.

modality: bedside bedroom light meter, actigraphy, PSQI
body:
This source is included for **free_living_observational_measurement**.

**Findings:** In 1,108 elderly HEIJO-KYO participants, PAL was defined as the 2-hour average bedroom light intensity before rise time. Sleep disturbance prevalence increased with PAL exposure. In adjusted models, the highest PAL quartile versus lowest had OR 1.65 for sleep disturbances (95% CI 1.16 to 2.34). Actigraphic sleep efficiency was 2.6% lower, wake after sleep onset 7.5 minutes longer, and sleep-onset latency 0.2 log-minutes longer in Q4 versus Q1.

**Why it matters:** It is timing-specific and unusually close to the morning window, but the exposure occurred before waking and was associated with worse rather than better sleep outcomes.

**Potential experiment signals:** 2-hour pre-rise light average, PSQI sleep disturbance, sleep efficiency, WASO, sleep-onset latency, chronotype.

**Population mismatch / directness:** Older adults and pre-awake bedroom light rather than adult post-wake outdoor light; association is adverse and observational. Directness: `same_mechanism`.

**Limitations:** cross-sectional; older-adult cohort; pre-awake exposure not post-wake outdoor exposure; possible chronotype and bedroom-window confounding; no causality.

**Protocol takeaway:** Treat as cautionary context: pre-awake bedroom light is not the same as deliberate morning outdoor light after wake-up.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

This source is included for **Exercise-timed whole-body PBM sibling variant**.

**Findings:** This recommendations paper is not a whole-body efficacy trial. Its main value is methodological: it argues that PBMT for exercise performance and post-exercise recovery has a therapeutic dose window and that future trials should follow stronger reporting standards such as CONSORT and TIDieR. It also notes that the existing evidence base has low-to-moderate certainty because of risk of bias and imprecision. For this protocol, it belongs in background context because the cited evidence is predominantly localized muscle PBM, not whole-body red and near-infrared exposure.

**Why it matters:** It helps explain why sports whole-body studies often borrow localized PBM assumptions and why dosing or reporting heterogeneity is a major limitation.

**Protocol takeaway:** Keep as background context only.

body:
This source is included for **Broader HIIT and VO2max context**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Meta-analysis of randomized HIIT protocol trials (2019).
- **People studied or addressed:** Healthy, overweight/obese, and athletic adults (about 1,514 pooled participants / 53 included studies).
- **Role in Murph:** broader programming context, not exact-dose proof.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy and the design logic behind using long aerobic intervals.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

It helps explain why 4-minute intervals are a plausible programming choice instead of just another arbitrary HIIT format.

## What it found

**Findings:** Across 53 randomized HIIT trials and about 1,514 pooled participants, HIIT improved VO2max overall. Subgroup analyses favored longer intervals, higher total interval volume, and programs lasting at least several weeks, which makes the 4-minute interval design more plausible—but the paper pooled many HIIT recipes rather than testing only Norwegian 4x4.

## How Murph should use it

Use it to support the design logic behind 4x4, not to claim that all HIIT evidence is exact 4x4 evidence.

## Important limits

This meta-analysis mixes protocols, populations, and comparators. It supports the broader family, not one exact home-experiment recipe.

## Plain-language takeaway

This is useful background for why long intervals make sense, but it is still one step removed from the exact “does Norwegian 4x4 work for me?” question.

**Findings:** Population: Patients with intrinsic circadian rhythm sleep disorders and selected neuropsychiatric illnesses with circadian/sleep dysregulation. Intervention/exposure: Light therapies including bright light, dark therapy, and dawn simulation across clinical indications. **Why it matters:** Useful as backbone context for clinical light-therapy boundaries and endpoints.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: Clinical sleep and neuropsychiatric disorders rather than healthy users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** Heterogeneous diagnoses and light protocols; mostly device-based or clinically supervised interventions; not outdoor morning-light habit evidence.

body:
This source is included for **Safety, contraindication, and population-boundary evidence**.

**Findings:** A systematic review searched Scopus, MEDLINE/PubMed, and Embase and included 27 articles covering PBMT for oral mucositis, lymphedema, radiodermatitis, and peripheral neuropathy in oncology settings. Most included studies reported no side effects with PBMT, and the review concluded that the current literature did not identify tumor-safety issues linked to supportive-care PBMT use. This is reassuring but still indirect for an unsupervised whole-body wellness protocol because the evidence base came from supervised oncology applications with heterogeneous designs and variable follow-up.

**Why it matters:** This is a backbone safety-only review for addressing cancer-related contraindication questions without turning supportive-care oncology PBMT into a whole-body efficacy claim.

**Potential experiment signals:** adverse events, tumor recurrence, cancer progression, treatment tolerability.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as clinical-supervised safety-boundary evidence: reassuring on observed oncology PBMT harms, but not direct proof for healthy-user whole-body protocols.

body:
This source is included for **Fatality mechanism context**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Review article (2019).
- **People studied or addressed:** Whitewater recreation and cold-water fatality context.
- **Role in Murph:** adjacent fatality mechanism context.
- **Directness to Cold Plunge:** adjacent variant fatality context.
- **Population mismatch:** High: whitewater recreation includes current, rescue, impact, and swimming demands that differ sharply from a controlled plunge.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** gasp, tachypnea, panic, palpitations, current/swimming demands vs stationary use.

## Findings

- The review proposes that some otherwise poorly explained cold-water 'flush drowning' cases in whitewater are manifestations of cold-water immersion syndrome.
- It notes that the initial cold-shock response begins in water below roughly 21–25°C and that the respiratory component includes an inhalational gasp followed by tachypnea that may exceed 60 breaths per minute.
- It also connects autonomic conflict with ectopic beats or arrhythmias and suggests that preparation, conditioning, and equipment may modify some responses.

## Limitations

- Adjacent whitewater fatality context rather than voluntary stationary plunges.
- Review article rather than direct cold-plunge trial.

## Why it matters

This source helps prevent a false sense of security about 'not-that-cold' water and reinforces that respiratory cold shock can be a primary fatality pathway.

## Potential experiment signals

- gasp
- tachypnea
- panic
- palpitations
- current/swimming demands vs stationary use

## Protocol takeaway

Use this as fatality-mechanism context only. It supports threshold and respiratory-hazard warnings, but it should not be treated as direct evidence about a stationary cold plunge protocol.

## Claim use

`safety-only`. Keep this source on the safety/context boundary rather than using it as direct efficacy support for the protocol.

body:
This source is included for **population_boundary_adjacent_claims**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** 2-year randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial (2020).
- **People studied or addressed:** Postmenopausal/older women with osteopenia.
- **Intervention/exposure:** Creatine monohydrate 3 g/day.
- **Comparator/control:** Placebo.
- **Duration/follow-up:** 2 years.
- **Role in Murph:** context-only / adjacent_variant.

## Findings

**Findings:** In 200 older women with osteopenia randomized to creatine monohydrate 3 g/day or placebo for 2 years, the trial reported no improvement in bone health, lean mass, or muscle function and no effect on health-related laboratory parameters [source_artifact:pmid-31257405].

## Why it matters

It is a long-duration, adequately sized null trial that prevents bone-health benefits from being overpromised. [source_artifact:pmid-31257405]

## Potential experiment signals

Bone-density, falls/fractures, lean mass, muscle function, and lab-parameter outcomes are relevant to a bone/subgroup variant, not to the default protocol claim stack [source_artifact:pmid-31257405].

## Protocol takeaway

Use as context-only null evidence for bone-health variants; do not translate into default protocol benefits or harms. [source_artifact:pmid-31257405]

## Key limitations and population mismatch

- Older women with osteopenia, not general adult gym users [source_artifact:pmid-31257405]
- Bone-health endpoints are outside default protocol scope [source_artifact:pmid-31257405]
- Adverse-event details were not fully extracted here beyond laboratory-parameter statement [source_artifact:pmid-31257405]
- Population mismatch: Osteopenia/bone-health trial in older women is an adjacent clinical/subgroup context. [source_artifact:pmid-31257405]

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Adjacent-variant and exclusion boundary anchors**.

**Findings:** This guideline concluded that specific PBM protocols can be recommended for prevention of oral mucositis and related pain in hematopoietic stem cell transplant, head-and-neck radiotherapy without chemotherapy, and head-and-neck radiotherapy with chemotherapy. It also concluded that no guideline was possible for treatment of established oral mucositis or for chemotherapy-only oral mucositis because evidence was inadequate and settings were too variable. Safety reporting in the analyzed randomized trials did not identify short- or long-term adverse events, although one cohort study reported a non-painful burning sensation in 15% of participants. Population mismatch is explicit: these are localized supervised oncology protocols, not whole-body wellness exposure.

**Why it matters:** It prevents localized oncology PBM protocols from being overgeneralized into whole-body claims and highlights the need to preserve parameter specificity.

**Potential experiment signals:** oral mucositis severity, oral pain, parameter fidelity, setting-specific safety.

**Protocol takeaway:** Treat this as a safety and clinical-supervision boundary source only. Parameter-specific oral-mucositis recommendations should not be ported into whole-body protocol copy.

**Claim use:** `safety-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Safety, contraindication, and population-boundary evidence**.

**Findings:** Two phase I single-blind dose-escalation randomized controlled trials exposed healthy volunteers' forearms to LED red light three times weekly for three weeks. STARS 1 randomized 60 participants across all skin types to 160-640 J/cm^2, and STARS 2 enrolled 55 non-Hispanic Caucasian participants at 480-640 J/cm^2. There were no serious adverse events, but predefined dose-limiting toxicities occurred at 480 J/cm^2 in STARS 1 and at 640 J/cm^2 in STARS 2, with blistering and prolonged erythema alongside milder transient erythema and hyperpigmentation. The authors concluded that safe upper bounds in these trials were 320 J/cm^2 for skin of color and 480 J/cm^2 for non-Hispanic Caucasian participants.

**Why it matters:** This is the strongest human safety anchor in the batch for red-light skin exposure and the clearest reminder that dose tolerance can vary across populations.

**Potential experiment signals:** erythema, hyperpigmentation, blistering, delayed skin recovery, session tolerability.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as same-mechanism human skin-safety evidence: high-fluence red light can produce dose-limiting skin reactions, so whole-body protocols should stay conservative and monitor skin response.

**Claim use:** `safety-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Adjacent-variant and exclusion boundary anchors**.

**Findings:** The review screened 871 records and included nine publications, with meta-analysis performed on six full-text publications in young healthy adults. The pooled estimate reported improved cognition with standardized mean difference 0.833 (95% CI 0.458 to 1.209) across 14 comparisons. At the same time, the authors reported heterogeneity, modest overall study quality, and funnel-plot or statistical signals consistent with publication bias. Population mismatch remains clear: this is transcranial head-only PBM in cognition studies, not whole-body exposure.

**Why it matters:** It is the main reason cognition claims need a scope boundary in a whole-body PBM protocol page.

**Potential experiment signals:** cognitive performance, attention, executive function, reaction time.

**Protocol takeaway:** Keep the result as transcranial cognition context only. It should not be used as direct evidence that whole-body red/NIR exposure improves cognitive performance.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **Adjacent-variant and exclusion boundary anchors**.

**Findings:** The meta-analysis reported improved depression scores with standardized mean difference -0.37 (95% CI -0.63 to -0.12) across 18 studies and 610 patients, and improved response rate with relative risk 1.42 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.85) across 16 studies and 559 patients. Reported adverse effects were generally mild to moderate and included headache, irritability or hypomanic symptoms, hyperactivity, nausea, eyestrain, insomnia, and nervousness. The authors also note important limitations: short study durations, small average sample sizes, heterogeneity in illumination and timing, and recurrent risk-of-bias concerns. Population and modality mismatch are explicit because this is bright-light treatment for seasonal affective disorder, not whole-body red/NIR photobiomodulation.

**Why it matters:** It keeps a legitimate positive light-therapy meta-analysis in the right intervention bucket and helps avoid wavelength or modality confusion.

**Potential experiment signals:** depression symptoms, response rate, headache, eyestrain, insomnia.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use only as bright-light mood-disorder context and adverse-effect boundary, not as direct PBM support.

body:
This source is included for **Winter-swimming acclimation and cardiovascular context**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** Literature review (2019).
- **People studied or addressed:** Winter swimmers and whole-body cold-water exposure context.
- **Role in Murph:** adjacent acclimation/cardiovascular context.
- **Directness to Cold Plunge:** adjacent winter-swimming context rather than direct plunge evidence.
- **Population mismatch:** High: winter swimmers experience a different exposure pattern and task demand than a short stationary plunge.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** adaptation history, entry symptoms, palpitations, time in cold water, whole-body stress tolerance.

## Findings

- The review describes winter swimming as a stressful whole-body cold exposure to which swimmers may acquire variable degrees of adaptation.
- It also notes that harmful effects remain possible and recommends a stepwise strategy to initiate and build up the activity.
- That makes it adjacent acclimation context, not a direct cold-plunge outcome source.

## Limitations

- Adjacent winter-swimming variant rather than stationary cold plunges.
- Review article rather than a defined protocol trial.

## Why it matters

This source is useful for acclimation and cardiovascular-context language, but it should not be promoted into direct evidence for a home plunge protocol.

## Potential experiment signals

- adaptation history
- entry symptoms
- palpitations
- time in cold water
- whole-body stress tolerance

## Protocol takeaway

Use this as adjacent acclimation context only: gradual build-up makes sense, but winter-swimming protection claims should stay separate from brief plunges.

`safety-only`. Keep this source on the safety/context boundary rather than using it as direct efficacy support for the protocol.

body:
This source is included for **Adjacent-variant and exclusion boundary anchors**.

**Findings:** The review describes intranasal PBM as either a nostril-based portable intervention or an implanted deep-nasal concept intended to deliver local or partially systemic effects. Accessible abstract text states that nostril-based intranasal PBM may improve blood rheology and cerebral blood flow and may resemble peripheral intravenous laser irradiation without puncture. The review also notes that no clinical studies of implanted deep-nasal PBMT had yet been conducted and that sham-controlled and transcranial-comparative studies were warranted. Population and modality mismatch are obvious because the exposure is local intranasal delivery rather than whole-body red/NIR exposure.

**Why it matters:** It helps keep intranasal device narratives from being mistaken for direct whole-body evidence.

**Potential experiment signals:** cerebral blood flow, blood rheology, neurologic symptoms, comparative sham response.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as same-mechanism context and boundary-setting only. Do not promote intranasal PBM findings into whole-body claims.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

body:
This source is included for **clinical_light_therapy_device_boundaries**.

**Findings:** Population: Patients with bipolar depression in randomized controlled light-therapy trials. Intervention/exposure: Adjunctive light therapy in bipolar depression. Comparator/control: Control light or other control conditions in included RCTs. Duration/follow-up: Varied by RCT Endpoints: depressive symptoms, clinical response, remission, acceptability, affective switches. Effect/direction: Seven trials representing 259 patients were identified. The review concluded evidence was positive but nonconclusive that adjunctive light therapy reduces bipolar depressive symptoms and increases clinical response. Safety/adverse events: No difference in affective switches was found between active light and control conditions (OR 1.30; 95% CI 0.38 to 4.44; p=0.67); the treatment was described as well tolerated.

**Why it matters:** High-priority safety boundary for bipolar-spectrum users.

**Potential experiment signals:** depression scores, response, remission, affective switch

**Protocol takeaway:** Clinical supervision is central; do not translate to self-directed outdoor light in bipolar disorder.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: Bipolar depression clinical trials, not general outdoor-light users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** Small samples; different light parameters; short treatment durations; variable trial quality; bipolar safety concerns.

body:
This source is included for **safety_boundaries**.

**Source key:** `source_artifact:pmid-31917880`.

**Findings:** Six RCTs evaluated bright-light therapy for bipolar depression. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in manic switching versus placebo/control (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.28 to 3.59) and reported no severe adverse events in the accessible abstract-level extraction.

**Why it matters:** Bipolar RCT meta-analysis found no significant increase in manic switching and no severe adverse events in the extracted evidence.

**Potential experiment signals:** manic switching, severe adverse events, depressive symptoms, remission.

**Protocol takeaway:** Light-based protocols should still include mania monitoring because confidence around rare switch events is limited by small trial counts.

**Claim use:** `safety-only`.

**Extraction notes:**

- **Participant count:** 6 (rcts_in_meta_analysis).
- **Population:** Patients with bipolar disorder in randomized trials of bright-light therapy.
- **Intervention or exposure:** Bright light therapy for bipolar depressive or manic symptoms.
- **Comparator or control:** Placebo or control conditions in included RCTs.
- **Duration or follow-up:** Literature through June 2019; trial durations varied.
- **Endpoints:** manic switching; severe adverse events; depressive symptoms; remission
- **Effect estimates or direction:** Six RCTs evaluated bright-light therapy for bipolar depression. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in manic switching versus placebo/control (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.28 to 3.59) and reported no severe adverse events in the accessible abstract-level extraction.
- **Adverse events or safety notes:** Aggregate RCT safety data are reassuring but imprecise; manic switch remains monitored.
- **Population mismatch:** Bipolar clinical population; relevant as a safety screen, not a direct outdoor protocol population.
- **Directness to Morning Outdoor Light Exposure:** Safety boundary. This source does not establish direct efficacy for the protocol variant.

**Directness and boundaries:** The source is safety-only here; efficacy findings are not promoted to the outdoor protocol.

**Limitations and uncertainty:**

- Few RCTs and imprecision around switch risk.
- No RCT evidence for recurrence prevention in euthymia or improving manic-state symptoms was extracted.
- Clinical bright-light therapy, not outdoor daylight.

body:
This source is included for **Safety and contraindications**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** American Heart Association scientific statement (2020).
- **People studied or addressed:** Adults considering moderate-to-vigorous or high-volume exercise.
- **Role in Murph:** safety and clinician-guidance boundary; supports safety boundaries; broad guideline context, not protocol-specific efficacy evidence.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy, session heart-rate fidelity, heart-rate recovery, symptoms and adherence.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

AHA scientific statement for acute cardiovascular event risk and progression language.

## What it found

**Findings:** The AHA statement emphasizes that regular physical activity lowers cardiovascular risk, while strenuous exercise can transiently raise acute event risk in susceptible people. That risk is especially relevant for inactive people or people with unrecognized disease starting vigorous exercise. The finding supports gradual progression and screening language.

## How Murph should use it

Supports caution language for symptoms, recent illness, heart disease, and other higher-risk situations.

Use to set screening, clinician-guidance, and stop-condition language; do not use it as evidence that unsupervised vigorous intervals are risk-free.

## Important limits

Guidelines frame risk management; they do not test the Murph 4x4 recipe.

The safe interpretation is narrower than “4x4 is always better.” Keep the population, supervision level, comparator, and exact interval dose visible before applying this source to a home wearable experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This is mainly a guardrail source: it helps decide who should get medical guidance, when to stop, and why screened supervision matters.

body:
This source is included for **Safety, contraindication, and population-boundary evidence**.

**Findings:** This short commentary responded to tumor-response concerns by arguing that in vivo and clinical studies with follow-up are more informative than isolated in vitro findings when assessing PBMT safety in cancer patients. It did not report new participants or new adverse-event data. Its value is interpretive: it helps set an evidence-hierarchy boundary, but it cannot by itself justify safety claims for whole-body red/NIR exposure.

**Why it matters:** It helps explain why Murph should weight human and animal follow-up data more heavily than isolated cell-culture concerns when discussing cancer-related safety questions.

**Potential experiment signals:** tumor progression concerns, recurrence surveillance, evidence-quality weighting.

**Protocol takeaway:** Treat as background commentary on evidence hierarchy, not as an independent safety or efficacy study.

**Claim use:** `safety-only`.

body:
This source is included for **strength_hypertrophy_trials**.

**Findings:** `source_artifact:pmid-32599716` — Physically active young adults took 0.0055 g/kg creatine or placebo after each training set during a six-week, five-day-per-week resistance-training program. Creatine improved leg press, chest press, total body strength, and leg press endurance; total body endurance improved in both groups but favored creatine. One participant reported gastrointestinal irritation during the first week.

**Why it matters:** Modern open-access direct trial with clear resistance-training endpoints and reported adverse-event/tolerability detail.

**Potential experiment signals:** leg press 1RM; chest press 1RM; total body strength; leg press endurance; total body endurance; GI irritation.

**Protocol takeaway:** Supports strength and muscular-endurance outcomes with creatine during a resistance-training program, but does not prove that intra-workout dosing is better than other creatine timing.

**Limitations and extraction boundary:** Small sample and below a priori power target. Intra-workout dosing was compared with placebo, not with morning, post-workout, or daily maintenance dosing. Population was young and physically active; results may not apply to older adults or clinical populations. Dietary creatine intake may not have been fully captured.

**Claim use:** `supports-protocol`.

body:
This source is included for **Safety and contraindications**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** European Society of Cardiology guideline (2021).
- **People studied or addressed:** People with cardiovascular disease considering exercise or sport.
- **Role in Murph:** safety and clinician-guidance boundary; supports safety boundaries; broad guideline context, not protocol-specific efficacy evidence.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy, session heart-rate fidelity, heart-rate recovery, symptoms and adherence.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

Backbone guideline for cardiovascular disease, exercise eligibility, and clinician-clearance boundaries.

## What it found

**Findings:** The ESC guideline treats exercise as beneficial for many cardiovascular conditions but makes eligibility disease- and risk-specific. Higher-intensity exercise is appropriate only when clinical status, risk category, and progression support it. The finding keeps Norwegian 4x4 out of unsupervised self-experiment territory for users with cardiovascular disease.

## How Murph should use it

Use it to keep clinician-clearance rules visible for known or suspected cardiovascular disease.

Use to set screening, clinician-guidance, and stop-condition language; do not use it as evidence that unsupervised vigorous intervals are risk-free.

## Important limits

The guideline is intentionally broader than this protocol and should not be treated as efficacy evidence.

The safe interpretation is narrower than “4x4 is always better.” Keep the population, supervision level, comparator, and exact interval dose visible before applying this source to a home wearable experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This is mainly a guardrail source: it helps decide who should get medical guidance, when to stop, and why screened supervision matters.

body:
This source is included for **clinical_light_therapy_device_boundaries**.

**Findings:** Population: Adults with bipolar depression in randomized adjunctive bright-light trials. Intervention/exposure: Adjunctive bright light therapy. Comparator/control: Control conditions in included RCTs. Duration/follow-up: Varied by RCT Endpoints: response, remission, manic switch, serious adverse effects. Effect/direction: Four trials with 190 participants were included. Response favored adjunctive bright light therapy (RR 1.78; 95% CI 1.24 to 2.56; p=0.002; I²=17%), while remission was not statistically significant (RR 2.03; 95% CI 0.48 to 8.59; p=0.34; I²=67%). Safety/adverse events: No serious adverse effects were reported; manic switch was 1.1% in bright light versus 1.2% in control in accessible extraction.

**Why it matters:** Preserves both efficacy and safety uncertainty in bipolar light therapy.

**Potential experiment signals:** response RR, remission RR, manic switch, serious adverse effects

**Protocol takeaway:** Response benefit should not be taken as unsupervised outdoor-light guidance for bipolar users.

**Directness and boundaries:** Directness is `clinical_supervised` with protocol-evidence scope `clinical_supervised`. Population mismatch: Bipolar depression clinical trials, not healthy outdoor-light users.

**Limitations and uncertainty:** Few small RCTs; heterogeneity for remission; short clinical trials; bipolar disorder safety context; device light not outdoor exposure.

**Claim use:** `context-only`.

**Why it matters:** This is a major mixed-evidence oncology review that helps keep theory-heavy tumor concerns separate from what has actually been observed in animal and human follow-up studies.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as safety-boundary context when malignancy is relevant: preclinical findings were mixed, but supervised in vivo and clinical evidence was more reassuring.

body:
This source is included for **Public health context**.

## Quick read

- **Source type:** World Health Organization physical-activity guideline (2020).
- **People studied or addressed:** Children, adolescents, adults, older adults, pregnant/postpartum people, and people living with chronic conditions or disability.
- **Role in Murph:** safety and clinician-guidance boundary; context only evidence; broad guideline context, not protocol-specific efficacy evidence.
- **Most relevant Murph signals:** estimated VO2max / cardio-fitness proxy, session heart-rate fidelity, heart-rate recovery, symptoms and adherence.

## Why it matters for Norwegian 4x4

Public-health context showing vigorous aerobic exercise as one option within weekly activity guidance.

## What it found

**Findings:** The WHO guideline recommends regular aerobic activity for adults and recognizes vigorous activity as one valid way to meet weekly targets. It also emphasizes reducing sedentary behavior and adapting activity to health status. The finding supports public-health context, not a specific 4x4 efficacy claim.

## How Murph should use it

Use as background that movement matters, while keeping Norwegian 4x4 as one bounded experiment.

Use to set screening, clinician-guidance, and stop-condition language; do not use it as evidence that unsupervised vigorous intervals are risk-free.

## Important limits

Public-health guidance is not evidence that high-intensity intervals are the best fit for every user.

The safe interpretation is narrower than “4x4 is always better.” Keep the population, supervision level, comparator, and exact interval dose visible before applying this source to a home wearable experiment.

## Plain-language takeaway

This is mainly a guardrail source: it helps decide who should get medical guidance, when to stop, and why screened supervision matters.

body:
This source is included for **free_living_observational_measurement**.

**Findings:** In 99 adolescents with evening circadian preference, lower average light intensity across the preceding 24 hours was associated with later sleep onset (p<0.01) and later next-day sleep offset (p<0.05). Later last exposure above 10 lux was associated with later sleep onset, shorter objective total sleep time, later bedtime, and shorter subjective total sleep time (all p<0.001 in extracted notes). Exploratory analyses linked lower early-morning light from 04:00-09:00 with later sleep onset, later next-day sleep offset, and later waketime.

**Why it matters:** It provides timing and threshold variables that may be useful for future self-tracking: early morning light and last exposure above 10 lux.

**Potential experiment signals:** 24-hour average light intensity, last exposure >10 lux, early morning light 04:00-09:00, sleep onset, sleep offset, total sleep time.

**Population mismatch / directness:** Adolescents with evening preference; not adult or outdoor-specific, and observational only. Directness: `adjacent_variant`.

**Limitations:** adolescent evening-preference sample; observational; threshold timing not an intervention; not outdoor-specific; multiple exploratory tests.

**Protocol takeaway:** Use as adjacent adolescent context for timing metrics; do not generalize to adult outdoor morning-light efficacy.
